adversarial_test_results.prompt:
Every autumn the county museum closes its public rooms for a week, and the staff move downstairs into the archive. The work is slow and dull. Boxes come up from the basement on a trolley, the lids are lifted, and every folder is checked against the accession register before it goes back on the shelf. Nobody enjoys the week, but the director insists, and so it passes in the smell of dust and old paper.

This year the archivist was a quiet woman named Ruth, who had come from a smaller museum up the coast. She worked without complaint and rarely spoke. By the third day she had cleared the whole of the east wall on her own. On the fourth morning she opened a box that was not listed in the register at all. It was plain and grey, tied with string, and inside were letters, a few photographs, and a ledger bound in green cloth.

The letters were ordinary enough. They concerned a shipping business, the price of coal, a disputed invoice, a wedding postponed twice. Ruth read a few and put them aside. The ledger was more interesting. Its pages were ruled in faint columns, and someone had entered each transaction in a careful hand, month by month, for eleven years. The dates ran from the spring of 1931 to the winter of 1942.

Around the middle of the volume the entries changed. The neat columns gave way to longer notes in the margin, and the writing grew hurried. Ruth turned the pages slowly. She had handled enough private papers to know when a record stops being a record and becomes something else, and this was one of those cases. The writer had begun to explain himself, and once he started he could not stop.

There were complaints about a foreman, an apology to a brother, a long account of a fire in a warehouse, and then, near the end of the book, a single sentence written across the full width of the sheet: the coal was never paid for, and I have carried that debt for thirty years. Ruth read it twice and sat still for a while.

The rest of the volume was blank. She photographed the page against the light, wrote the number of the box in her notebook, and carried it upstairs to the director, who listened, nodded, and asked whether it was worth anything. Ruth said she did not think so. It was only one sentence, after all, and the writer was long dead, and the company he had worked for had closed before either of them was born. But she kept a copy on her desk for the rest of the winter.

After the holidays a researcher from the university wrote to ask about the collection, and Ruth sent him a short description of the box. He replied within a week, wanting to know more. She answered each question in turn, politely, and said nothing about the sentence on the last page. Some things belong to the person who found them, she thought, at least for a while.
